disease_info: Bipolar I Disorder is characterized by at least one lifetime manic episode, typically lasting at least one week and causing clear functional impairment, often alternating with episodes of major depression. Manic episodes involve markedly elevated or irritable mood with increased energy and activity, while depressive episodes feature low mood and loss of energy or interest, both often accompanied by cognitive and sleep changes. The course is usually recurrent and episodic, with periods of relative euthymia in between, and episodes can be triggered or amplified by psychosocial stress, sleep disruption, or substance use. It is distinguished from Bipolar II by the presence of full mania rather than hypomania, and from unipolar depression by the history of manic episodes and frequently a stronger family loading for bipolar spectrum conditions.

narrative.personality: Tristan is a highly organized, imaginative, and socially engaged young man who thrives on creative projects and group activities while carefully managing his responsibilities and finances.
narrative.stressor: The onset of Tristan’s difficulties began after he was promoted to supervise a larger home‑care team while simultaneously spearheading a new art‑based enrichment program his agency hoped to showcase to funders. Eager to prove himself and build a portfolio for future graduate applications, he started stretching his workdays late into the evening, saying yes to every committee, and filling his off‑hours with planning pop‑up installations and new workshops. Over a couple of weeks, the combination of mounting deadlines, constant emails, and back‑to‑back community events led to a pattern of increasingly disorganized days at work, missed details in client schedules, and tension with staff who felt he was scattered and unreliable, which was a stark contrast to his usual meticulous style. When a senior manager formally documented his performance and a close friend pulled him aside to say they were worried about how “all over the place” he had become, he agreed—reluctantly at first—to see a psychiatrist because he felt his attention and day‑to‑day control were slipping away from him.
narrative.chief_complaint: “My attention keeps jumping all over the place and I can’t seem to stay focused on what actually matters.”

narrative.personality: Brenetta is a warm, community‑minded elder who likes structure and traditions, worries carefully over practical details, and takes pride in organizing church and neighborhood activities.
narrative.stressor: Brenetta’s current episode emerged in the months after the death of her closest church friend, a woman she had sung beside in the choir and planned potlucks with for decades. In trying to fill the void, she threw herself into every available church responsibility—taking on extra choir rehearsals, additional quilting sessions, and more hosting than usual—telling others she was fine as long as she stayed busy. Over time, the combination of grief, disrupted routines, and constant interpersonal friction as she became more impatient with minor disagreements led to growing tension with choir members and family, who noticed that her usually gentle leadership had become unusually sharp, demanding, and difficult to redirect. After a heated argument at a church meeting that left her embarrassed and several congregants upset, her pastor and a niece gently urged her to see a doctor, and she agreed because she was disturbed by how uncharacteristically “worked up and on edge” she felt most of the time.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Lately I’m on edge all the time and getting upset with people over every little thing.”

narrative.personality: Nancy is a calm, curious, and methodical teacher who enjoys carefully planned bilingual lessons, outdoor exploration, and reflective practices like yoga and reading.
narrative.stressor: Nancy’s problems began during a particularly demanding school year when her district rolled out a new bilingual curriculum and she volunteered to pilot it while also serving on the implementation committee. She started staying late to rewrite lesson plans, attending evening training sessions, and using weekends to prep materials, all while trying to maintain her usual commitments to yoga, hiking, and volunteer tutoring. Over a couple of weeks, the sustained pressure and long days gradually eroded her usual sense of balance; she found herself dragging through classes, falling behind on grading, and needing colleagues to cover for her when she felt too drained to manage group work, which was unsettling for someone typically seen as dependable and steady. When she realized that her exhaustion was persisting despite attempting to rest over a school break and that her performance evaluations were starting to slip, she sought psychiatric help, worried that something more than regular work stress was sapping her energy and effectiveness.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I feel exhausted all the time, no matter how much I rest, and I don’t have the energy to get through my school day.”
